## Principles

1. **One fact, one place.** A fact about the project lives where a change
   keeps it true: in the code, or in a comment at the one place that uses
   it. To change a fact, change it where it lives. Before you write it
   anywhere new, delete it from where it was.
2. **Only current knowledge is in reach.** What stops being true is
   deleted, not marked as old. History is kept in archived items and
   commits, and it describes the project at that commit. Never read it as
   the current state.
3. **Every domain change is an item.** An item is the self-contained record
   of one change: why it was made, the check agreed for it, and the proof.
   It is linked to its commits, and the items together are the project's
   history.
4. **Say what you expect before any work.** Before work starts, you and the
   user agree on what the result must show. Only that check judges the
   result.
5. **The user sees it work.** An item is proven when the user has seen it
   work, shown live. Any other claim rests on what a command printed. A
   summary or a reading of the code is not proof.
6. **The user decides; the agent proposes.** A question that only the user
   can answer is parked, never assumed.

## Processes and files

The user and other sessions run processes on this machine too.

- Stop a process only by the id of a process that you started. Never stop
  a process by a name or a pattern: `pkill -f` also stops the processes of
  the user and of other sessions.
- Put each file that you create outside the worktree in a directory that
  `mktemp -d` makes. Never write to a fixed path in `/tmp`.
- When you no longer need a process or a file that you started or created,
  stop it or delete it. An agent that workbench starts does this before it
  returns. The item's session does it at the latest before
  `workbench merge`.

## Where knowledge lives

- A fact about the project that one place in the code can hold lives in
  the code, or in a comment at that place. When the fact changes, change it
  there. A comment holds only a fact that the code cannot show. Never write
  a comment or a doc comment that restates the code or the signature below
  the comment.
- A fact that no single place in the code can hold, such as a flow across
  files, a contract between parts, or why a simpler design was not taken,
  lives in `CLAUDE.md` in the deepest directory that covers it. Change it in
  the same commit as its code.
- What a domain word means lives in `workbench/GLOSSARY.md`. When the meaning
  changes, change the entry.
- A fact that no commit can make wrong, such as the user, their machine, or
  how they want work done, lives in agent memory. When it is wrong, delete
  it. Agent memory is kept in the main checkout, so each change to it shows
  in the diff there. Never commit a change to it: the user reviews each
  change and commits or reverts it.
- An idea lives in `workbench/BACKLOG.md`, as one entry. When the idea
  becomes an item or is dropped, delete the entry.
- Work in progress lives in its open item until the item is archived.
- What was true at a commit lives in archived items and commits, and is
  kept.

Read history only to answer one question, for example why something is the
way it is, before you change it or reverse an earlier decision. Never read
it to learn how the project works now. A fact from history can be false:
verify it before you use it, in reasoning or in code. When items disagree,
the open item wins, then the newest archived item, then each older one.
When history disagrees with the code, the code wins.

## Items

An item is one change to what the project does for its users: a bug fix, a
new or different behaviour, or making it faster. Create the item before you
write code for the change.

Work that changes nothing the project does is housekeeping, for example
cleanup, restructuring, configs, tooling and agent settings. Housekeeping
gets no item and goes straight to main. Before you start, agree with the
user what the result must show. Write the reason in the commit message. The
project's own checks must still pass. A restructure that an item needs is
part of that item.

Pick the kind by what is known now:

| Kind | When | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| bug | the project does something wrong today | Why, Root cause, Check, Proof |
| feature | the project should do something new or different | Why, Check, Proof |
| spike | an area that is not understood well enough to say what the result must show | Why, Questions, Findings |

An idea that nobody opens now is an entry in `workbench/BACKLOG.md`, not
an item.

A spike's findings are claims. Before a feature builds on a finding, verify
the finding.

Everything a spike builds goes in the folder beside its item,
`workbench/items/<id>/`, and nowhere else. A merged spike stays on
main until the user drops it. A feature that builds on a spike names the
spike's id in its Why. Nothing outside the spike's folder refers to the
spike's files, in code or in text, because dropping the spike deletes
them.

## Check and proof

The check is the list of steps that judges an item. Each step is one of:

- a command, and the output it must print;
- what the user must see, when only the user can judge it, for example
  how something looks or feels.

The check holds only steps and their expected results, no reasoning and no
design.

The item's scope is what the item must change. In a bug, the scope is each
behaviour that the root cause makes wrong in the way that the Why
describes. In a feature, the scope is each change that the Why asks for,
and what each new thing does, invalid input included. A behaviour that
worked before the change is in the scope only if the Why asks to change it.

If the check has no step for a case in the scope, decide what the project
does in that case. Follow the way the project handles similar cases. In
the item's session, do not ask the user about such a case before the demo.
Write each such decision in the proof, with the command that shows it. At
the demo, `wb-demo` shows and records each such decision in the same way
as a step.
If the user wants a different behaviour, agree a step for it with the user.

An existing behaviour is a behaviour that the project had before the
change and that is outside the item's scope. If you are not sure that a
behaviour is in the scope, treat it as an existing behaviour. If the check
has no step for an existing behaviour, keep that behaviour as it was
before the change. This rule also holds when you fix a review finding. If
you cannot keep that behaviour, stop and ask the user. If the user accepts
that behaviour as it is after the change, agree a step for it with the
user.

In the item's session of a bug or a feature, you can find a behaviour
that was already wrong before the change. If that behaviour is outside the
item's scope and the check has no step for it:

- Add an entry for the behaviour to `workbench/BACKLOG.md`.
- Commit the entry on the item's branch.
- At the demo, `wb-demo` shows the user each entry that the item's branch
  adds to `workbench/BACKLOG.md`.
- If the user agrees a step for the behaviour, delete the entry.

While you keep the behaviour:

- do not ask the user a question about the behaviour or about the entry;
- do not offer or propose a change to the behaviour, in this item or in
  another item.

An entry in `workbench/BACKLOG.md` is not a decision about what the
project must do. The user decides later whether the entry becomes an
item.

Each step must be able to fail. Before you change anything, make sure
that each step that checks what the project does now fails:

- Run each command step, and see it fail.
- Show the user each step that only the user can judge, or let the user
  do the step. The user says if the step fails.

A step that passes before the change proves nothing: agree a new step with
the user.

A step judges the change from outside it. It runs the project as its users
do, or a tool or test that exists before the change. Never accept a step
that runs a test or script that the item adds. Such a step proves nothing.

For each command step of a bug's or a feature's check, add a test that
covers that step and no other step. Write each test at the highest level
that shows the step reliably. A test is reliable if it gives the same
result each time that it runs on the same code. The levels, from the
highest:

- through the project, as its users use it;
- across the parts of the project;
- in one part alone.

In one of these cases, write no test for the step, also in a bug:

- No level shows the step reliably. For example, at each level, the
  test of the step depends on the network.
- The test needs something that no other test of the project uses. For
  example, the test needs a database, a service or a browser.

A test with a fake in place of the network or a service is reliable if
the fake is in a test file. If such a test shows the step, write that
test.

For each step that has no test because of one of these cases, write
`No test: <step> — <why>` under the item's title. In <why>, name the
case and why the case is true for the step. `wb-judge` checks each such
line.

At each level, the test uses the code as the project uses the code.
Never add code that only tests use to the project's code. Put such code,
for example a fake, a stub or a mock, in a test file or in a file that
only tests load.

Never take the expected result of a test from a run of the code, by hand
or by a snapshot. Write it from the step that the test covers.

The test keeps the step true for later items. The test is never the
item's proof.

For a bug, write each test before you fix the bug. Change and run the
test until it fails on the step's expected result and for no other
reason. After that, change only the code until the test passes.

For a feature, write each test after its step works. Once the test
passes, commit all of your changes. Then break the code. To break the
code, make the smallest change after which the project no longer gives
the step's expected result. Run the test and see it fail on that result.
If it passes, change the test until the break makes it fail. Then undo
the break with `git checkout` of each file that the break changed. After
that, `git status` must show no change.

If a test that main had when the item's branch started fails, fix the
code until the test passes. Test data and test runners count as tests
here. Change or delete such a test only if the item changes the behaviour
that the test checks. Then write in the proof which test changed, why its
old expected result is wrong now, and which line of the item says so. To
add a test to a file of such tests does not change them.

Stop and ask the user before you change such a test for another reason.
Also stop and ask before you change a test of a bug after the test failed
on its step's expected result. If the user agrees, write in the proof
which test changed, why, and what the user said.

A test that passes and fails on the same code shows nothing. Never run
the test again to get a pass. Stop. Show the user the output of a pass
and the output of a fail. The user decides what to do next.

The check is fixed when the user agrees it. If a step misses its expected
result and you cannot make it pass, record the miss in the proof, with
what the step showed. Never reword the step. Stop and ask the user,
who picks one of these:

- accept the miss;
- agree a new step, while the missed step and its output stay in the proof;
- drop the item.

If a step can be shown only after the merge, for example because it needs
the change deployed or an event that you cannot cause, ask the user, who
picks one of these:

- accept it unproven: write `Unproven: <step> — <why>` under the item's
  title;
- wait for it: write `Awaiting: <step> — <what it waits for>` under the
  item's title. The item stays open after the merge. When the step can
  be shown, start the item again, show the step to the user, write its
  proof and what the user said, and delete the line, then merge. If the
  step fails, fix it in the same item.

A decision line is a `No test:`, `Slow test:`, `Unproven:` or `Awaiting:`
line. For each change to the Why, the Check or a decision line, write in
the proof what the user said. Write it in the user's words, with the date
that the user said it. A `No test:` line that you write for one of the
cases above needs no words of the user.

The proof is the demo. After the review, `wb-demo` shows the user each
step of the check live. `wb-demo` is an agent that did not write the code.
It runs each command where the user sees it run, or it lets the user do
the step. It gives its own verdict on each step, and asks for the verdict
of the user. For each step, it writes in the proof the output, its
verdict, what the user said in the user's words, and the date.

If you showed the user a step before the change, write in the proof what
the user said then, and the date. Before the demo, paste in the proof, as
it was printed:

- for a command step that checks what the project does now: its output
  before the change;
- for each test: the output of the run in which it failed on its step's
  expected result, before the change or on the broken code;
- for each review finding that you fixed: its command, its output before
  the fix, and its output after the fix. If the command runs a script
  outside the repository, also paste the script.

Paste each command as you ran it, and its whole output. Never shorten or
rewrite either, except to replace a secret. Paste each output when it is
printed. A compact or a new session loses an output that is not in the
proof.

A step that the user did not see is not proven. A summary or a table
typed by hand is not proof. Replace each secret with `<REDACTED>`.

## Decisions

The user decides what the project must do, what its words mean, what an
item must show, and whether work ships or stops. You decide how to make a
change that the user agreed. You also decide each case in the item's scope
that the check has no step for.

When a decision is the user's, ask the user. Give the options you see, the
one you propose, and why. Until the user answers, do no work that the
answer changes. Never answer the question yourself. Never drop it because
later work made it look unnecessary.
Ask through the question prompt of your environment, when it has one,
so that the question shows as waiting.

Write the answer where it changes something: in the item, in the glossary,
or in the commit message.

When the user refuses a permission that you asked for, that is the user's
answer. Never look for another way to do what was refused.

## The life of an item

1. `workbench new <kind> "<title>"` writes the item on main and picks its
   id. With the user, write Why and agree the check (a spike: its
   questions).
2. `workbench start <id>` commits the item, creates the branch `<id>` or
   uses it if it already exists here or on the remote, makes the worktree
   `.worktrees/<id>` from it, and opens a session for the item there.
   From then on, the item changes only on its branch.
3. In the item's session, commit the item together with the code after
   each step that works, so that the branch holds all of the work.
4. For a bug or a feature, when the change is complete and committed,
   run `workbench ready <id>`. Then end your turn. `wb-reviewer` then
   reviews the branch, and workbench tells you what to do next. When your
   changes after a review, to the code or to the Why, the Check or a
   decision line, are complete and committed, run `workbench ready <id>`
   again. Then end your turn. Never start `wb-reviewer` or `wb-judge`
   yourself.
5. When workbench tells you to, run `workbench demo <id>`. The command
   opens a session of `wb-demo` in its own tmux window, `<id>-demo`. Then
   end your turn. Do not change anything in the worktree until `wb-demo`
   tells you how the demo went. Never show the demo yourself.
   - If the demo passed, ask the user if the item merges. If the user
     says yes, run `workbench merge`.
   - If a step failed, or the user or `wb-demo` found a problem, fix each
     failure and each problem on the branch as you fix a review finding.
     Then run `workbench ready <id>` again. If you cannot make a step
     pass, do as "Check and proof" says for a step that misses its
     expected result. If the user wants a new step, agree the step with
     the user.
6. `workbench merge <id> "<subject>"` runs `workbench/checks`, the
   project's own checks, in the item's worktree, if that file exists.
   Then it squashes the branch onto main as one commit with the trailer
   `Item: <id>`, and removes the branch and the worktree. A merged bug or
   feature moves to `workbench/items/archive/` in that commit, unless it
   has an `Awaiting:` line. A merged spike stays in `workbench/items/`
   with its folder.
7. `workbench drop <id> "<why>"` writes `Dropped: <why>` under the item's
   title and moves the item to the archive on main. It removes what the
   item still has: its branch and worktree, or a merged spike's folder.

## Code

Write the minimum code that the change needs.

If the change adds a second way to do a task that the code already does,
keep one way. Move each caller to the way that you keep. Delete the other
way in the same change.

If the code does not show what a number or a text means, define that
value as a named constant.
